title: "Part 3 — Git and GitHub"
subtitle: "Keeping your work, and getting it back"
---

Git answers a question that you will ask at some point: *what did this look
like before I broke it?*

::: {.callout-tip}
## Most of this page is executed

Each time this site is built, everything before the GitHub section runs on a
real repository. Git works completely on your own computer. It uses the
internet only when you connect to a server.
:::

# The problem

You have `analysis.py`. You change it. It stops working, and you cannot remember
what you changed.

Many people then create `analysis_v2.py`, then `analysis_final.py`, then
`analysis_final_REALLY.py`. The result is a folder where nobody can tell which
file produced which result.

Git replaces all of this with one directory that remembers **every version of
every file in it**, and who changed what, when, and why.

# Setting up

Git saves a name and an email address with every change. So tell Git once who
you are:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.org"
```

`--global` means "for every repository on this computer", so you do this only
once.

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

This sets the name of the first branch. `main` is the usual name today.

# A repository

A **repository** (dt. *Repositorium*, usually only *repo*) is a directory that
Git watches. Create one:

```bash
mkdir myanalysis
cd myanalysis
git init
```

```text
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/user1/myanalysis/.git/
```

This created a hidden `.git` directory. **This directory is the repository**:
the whole history is stored there. If you delete it, you have ordinary files
again.

Now create a file for Git to track:

```bash
echo "print('hello')" > analysis.py
git status
```

Git reports `analysis.py` as **untracked**: Git can see the file, but does not
watch it yet.

# The three steps

In Git, saving your work has three steps, not one. This is intended.

```bash
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Add the analysis script"
```

```text
[main (root-commit) 9c1f2ab] Add the analysis script
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

| step | what it means |
|---|---|
| edit | change files as usual |
| `git add` | choose what goes into the next snapshot ("staging") |
| `git commit` | take the snapshot, with a message saying why |

The middle step looks unnecessary, but it is useful: you can commit *some* of
your changes and leave the rest for later. So two unrelated fixes become two
commits with two clear messages, not one commit called "stuff".

::: {.callout-tip}
## Write the message for the person reading it later

That person is you, in six months, when you try to find where something broke.

"Fix bug" tells the reader nothing. "Fix the off-by-one error that dropped the
last row" takes ten seconds more, and it helps. Say **why**, not what: the diff
already shows what changed.
:::

## Seeing what happened

```bash
echo "print('goodbye')" >> analysis.py
git status --short
```

```text
 M analysis.py
```

`M` means modified. To see the change itself:

```bash
git diff
```

```text
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 print('hello')
+print('goodbye')
```

Lines with `+` were added, and lines with `-` were removed. Commit the change:

```bash
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Say goodbye as well as hello"
git log --oneline
```

```text
4d5e6f7 Say goodbye as well as hello
9c1f2ab Add the analysis script
```

This list of versions is the reason to use Git.

::: {.callout-important}
## Do not commit data

Git is built for text: code, scripts, notes, configuration. It does not work
well with large binary files. Git keeps every version forever, so if you commit
a 2 GB dataset once, it stays in the repository permanently, even after you
delete it.

Keep data outside the repository, or list it in a file called `.gitignore`:

```bash
printf "results/\n*.csv\n" > .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Ignore results and data files"
```

Now Git no longer offers to track these files. **A repository should contain
everything that is needed to *reproduce* the results** — including `pixi.toml`
and `pixi.lock` from Part 2 — but not the results themselves.
:::

# Going back

This is the reason for everything above. To discard changes that you have not
committed:

```bash
echo "print('a terrible mistake')" >> analysis.py
git restore analysis.py
git diff
```

`git diff` prints nothing: the file is back in its last committed state, and
the mistake is gone.

To look at an old version without changing anything:

```bash
git show HEAD~1:analysis.py
```

```text
print('hello')
```

`HEAD` is where you are now, and `HEAD~1` is one commit before it. Nothing was
changed: Git only read an old version from its history.

# Branches

A **branch** is a separate line of work. On a branch, you can try something
risky without changing what already works:

```bash
git switch -c experiment
echo "print('a new idea')" >> analysis.py
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Try a new idea"
```

`-c` creates the branch and moves you to it. To see which branches exist, and
which one you are on:

```bash
git branch
```

```text
  experiment
* main
```

The `*` marks where you are. The first line of `git status` says the same. This
is why you should read `git status` before you do anything else.

Switch back:

```bash
git switch main
cat analysis.py
```

```text
print('hello')
print('goodbye')
```

The new idea is not here. It is on the branch `experiment`, unchanged. To keep
it:

```bash
git merge experiment
cat analysis.py
```

```text
print('hello')
print('goodbye')
print('a new idea')
```

Or, to drop it, do not merge it.

```bash
git log --oneline --graph --all
```

## Merge conflicts

If the same lines changed on both branches, Git cannot decide which version you
want, and it tells you so. This is not rare. Beginners meet it early, especially
in a small team where two people edit the same file in the same week.

::: {.callout-note}
## These commands are not executed automatically

A conflict needs two branches that disagree on purpose. A build script should
not create that on every run. So this example is shown, but not run
automatically. Every command and every line of output below is real: we ran
these exact commands once and copied the result.
:::

Two branches, each changing the same line differently:

```{.bash .no-run}
git switch -c change-greeting-a
printf "print('hi there')\nprint('goodbye')\nprint('a new idea')\n" > analysis.py
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Change the greeting to 'hi there'"

git switch main
printf "print('hey!')\nprint('goodbye')\nprint('a new idea')\n" > analysis.py
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Change the greeting to 'hey!'"
```

Merge them:

```{.bash .no-run}
git merge change-greeting-a
```

```text
Auto-merging analysis.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in analysis.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

Git could not decide, so it stopped and put both versions in the file:

```{.bash .no-run}
cat analysis.py
```

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
print('hey!')
=======
print('hi there')
>>>>>>> change-greeting-a
print('goodbye')
print('a new idea')
```

Everything above `=======` comes from your current branch (`HEAD`). Everything
below it comes from the branch that you are merging, and the marker line names
that branch. Only the lines that disagree are marked like this. The rest of the
file is unchanged.

Edit the file so that it says what you want, and delete all three marker lines.
`<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` are not part of your file: Git added them
only to show you the conflict:

```{.bash .no-run}
printf "print('hey there')\nprint('goodbye')\nprint('a new idea')\n" > analysis.py
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Resolve the greeting conflict"
```

This is all that a conflict is: Git does not guess, and you tell it what you
meant. `git add` marks the file as resolved, and `git commit` finishes the
merge. These are the same two steps as for any other change. A conflict does
not mean that anything is broken.

::: {.callout-tip}
## `git status` orients you mid-conflict too

If you get lost during a conflict, `git status` names the file with the
conflict and tells you what to do next. Here, as everywhere in Git, read
`git status` first.
:::

# GitHub

Everything so far happened on your own computer. **GitHub** is a website that
stores Git repositories. With it, you can keep a backup, work on more than one
computer, and show your work to other people. GitHub is not Git. It is one of
several such websites; GitLab is another one.

::: {.callout-important}
## You will need an account

If your practical uses a shared repository, at least one person in the team
needs a GitHub account, so that the repository can exist. In practice everyone
needs one: each of you pushes your own commits, and every commit is linked to
the account that made it.

An account is free, and you can create one in a minute:
[github.com/join](https://github.com/join). Do this before you need it, not
during a session. See also *"Make a GitHub profile, and treat it as one"*
below: an account is more than a requirement for the practical.
:::

@fig-git-stages shows everything on this page in one picture. It also adds the
part that GitHub is for: a **remote repository**, which is a copy of the same
history on a server instead of on your computer.

![The four stages a change passes through, and the command that moves it from
one to the next.](../figures/git-stages.svg){#fig-git-stages
fig-alt="Four boxes in a row: Workspace, Staging area, Local repository and
Remote repository. Workspace connects to Staging area via git add, Staging area
to Local repository via git commit, and Local repository to Remote repository
via git push. A dashed arrow labelled git pull or git clone runs from Remote
repository back to Workspace."}

`git push` and `git pull` are the two new commands. `git push` sends your local
history to the remote repository. `git pull` gets what changed there. `git
clone` is what you use the first time, instead of `git pull`: it does not update
an existing local repository, but creates a new one by copying the whole history
of the remote repository.

::: {.callout-note}
## The commands below are not executed

Unlike the rest of this page, these commands need an account, a login and a
real server. So they are shown, but not run automatically.
:::

Create an empty repository on the GitHub website. Then connect your local
repository to it:

```{.bash .no-run}
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/myanalysis.git
git push -u origin main
```

`origin` is the usual name for "the server that this repository came from".
After the first push, one word sends later commits:

```{.bash .no-run}
git push
```

To get changes that were made somewhere else:

```{.bash .no-run}
git pull
```

To start from someone else's repository instead:

```{.bash .no-run}
git clone https://github.com/someone/theirproject.git
cd theirproject
```

`clone` copies the whole history, not only the current files. So you get every
version, and you can work without the internet immediately.

## The everyday loop

```{.bash .no-run}
git pull                          # get what others changed
# ... do some work ...
git add .
git commit -m "Describe what you did"
git push                          # send it back
```

# Working in a shared repository

If several people share one repository and all commit to `main`, you will see
this in the first hour:

```text
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
```

Someone else pushed while you were working. Nothing is broken and nothing is
lost: Git refuses to overwrite their work with yours. Run `git pull`, resolve
any conflicts, then push again. A conflict after `git pull` looks the same as
the [merge conflict](#merge-conflicts) above, and you resolve it in the same
way, because `pull` is only `fetch` plus `merge`.

This works, but it becomes tiring. And every unfinished change goes directly
onto the branch that everyone else uses. The usual solution is the one from the
section on branches: **work on a branch, and merge it when it is ready.**

## Branch, push, pull request

```bash
git switch -c add-quality-filter
```

Do the work and commit it as usual. Then push **the branch**, not `main`:

```{.bash .no-run}
git push -u origin add-quality-filter
```

`-u` links your local branch to the branch on the server. After that,
`git push` alone is enough.

Then open a **pull request** (PR) on GitHub. The name is confusing: you do not
pull anything. A PR asks for *your* branch to be merged into `main`, and it
gives the team a place to discuss the change first.

::: {.callout-note}
## This part is done in the browser

After you push a branch, GitHub shows a **Compare & pull request** button on the
main page of the repository. Click it. Check that the base branch is `main` and
the compare branch is yours. Give the PR a title and one sentence that says what
it does, and create it.

Everyone in the team can then read the change and comment on single lines. When
the team agrees, someone clicks **Merge pull request**. After that, go back to
your terminal and run:

```{.bash .no-run}
git switch main
git pull
```

so that your local `main` also contains the merged change.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## The exact buttons move

GitHub changes its website often. So the names and positions above tell you
what to look for; they may not be exactly where you click. The steps do not
change: push a branch, open a request to merge it, agree, merge.
:::

## Why use branches in a small team

There are three reasons, and they are true even for two people:

- **`main` always works.** Unfinished work stays on a branch, so nobody else
  gets it.
- **Someone reads the change.** In a PR, a second person checks the change, and
  a person finds more errors than any tool.
- **It records the reasons.** The discussion stays linked to the change. So in
  six months, the repository answers *why*, not only *what*.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Keep pull requests small

People read a PR that changes one thing carefully. A PR that changes nineteen
things gets approved without real attention, and then the review is useless.
So merge often, in small steps.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Make a GitHub profile, and treat it as one

It is free, and it grows over time. A practical that you did well — a
repository with a clear README, code that runs, and an environment file that
lets someone reproduce it — is a real example of your work. It can be the first
item in your portfolio.

This is a much better reason to write good commit messages than an instruction
from a teacher.

**Take this seriously.** A GitHub profile can become your personal web page:
pinned repositories, a short biography, links to papers or projects, and even
its own website at `username.github.io`. Here is one good example:
[github.com/jonas-fuchs](https://github.com/jonas-fuchs), the profile of a
bioinformatician, built in this way. When you apply for a job in this field,
such a profile can say more than a CV. It shows that you can do the work,
instead of only claiming it.

You do not need to finish this during one semester. But *start* this semester:
a profile with one good repository is better than a profile with none, and it
only improves when you add to it.
:::

# When it goes wrong

**"Please tell me who you are."** You skipped the `git config` step above.

**You committed something by mistake.** If you have not pushed it,
`git reset --soft HEAD~1` undoes the commit and keeps the changes. If you *have*
pushed it — especially a password or a key — treat it as public. The fix is to
change the password or key, not to change the history. If you remove a commit
from a public repository, everyone who already has a copy still has it.

**`git push` is rejected.** Someone else pushed first. Run `git pull`, resolve
any conflicts, then push again.

**You are lost.** `git status` almost always tells you where you are and what you
should do next. Read it before you do anything that you cannot undo.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Be careful with advice from the internet

If you search the internet for a Git error, you will almost always find
`git reset --hard` and `git push --force`. Both can delete work permanently,
and both are usually the wrong answer to a beginner's problem.

`git status` and `git log` never delete anything. Start with them.
:::

# What you should be able to do now

- [ ] Have a GitHub account.
- [ ] Explain why `analysis_final_REALLY.py` is not version control.
- [ ] Configure your name and email.
- [ ] Make a repository and commit a file to it.
- [ ] Say what `add` does that `commit` does not.
- [ ] Write a commit message that helps the reader.
- [ ] See what changed with `git status`, `git diff` and `git log`.
- [ ] Recover a file you broke but had not committed.
- [ ] Say why data does not belong in a repository, and what does.
- [ ] Make a branch, commit on it, list branches, and merge it back.
- [ ] Recognise a merge conflict, resolve it by hand, and finish the merge.
- [ ] Push to GitHub and pull from it.
- [ ] Say what to do when a push is rejected.
- [ ] Push a branch and open a pull request from it.
